title: Choosing a tool for a task

sections.skill: Choose a tool from stated needs, limits and costs

questions.prompt: Where should tool choice start?

choices.text: With whichever brand is most famous, since famous tools are always best for every task

questions.correct_answer: With the task
questions.intro: Choosing a tool works best when you start from the TASK, not the brand. List your NEEDS (what it must do, such as read PDFs or handle your language), your LIMITS (budget, privacy rules, devices, approved tools) and how you will judge QUALITY (try it on a few real examples). Compare options against that list. Also count SWITCHING COSTS: time to learn a new tool and move your files, prompts or workflows. Avoid UNNEEDED SUBSCRIPTIONS: a tool you already have, or a free option, may be enough, and paying for three similar tools is common waste.

sections.skill: Compare options with a needs table

questions.prompt: Which option fails on cost?

choices.text: Z, because three dollars a month is more than the budget of five dollars a month

questions.correct_answer: X
questions.intro: Make a NEEDS TABLE. Rows: each need or limit. Columns: each option. Mark yes or no, and add costs. Cross out any option that fails a MUST-HAVE need. Among the rest, prefer the cheapest that does the job well. Example: must-haves are "works offline" and "under 5 dollars a month." Option X: offline yes, 8 dollars. Option Y: offline no, free. Option Z: offline yes, 3 dollars. X fails on cost, Y fails offline, so choose Z.

questions.prompt: Which option fails "works offline"?

choices.text: X, since paid options never work offline because they need to check your payment

questions.prompt: A vendor's demo looks amazing. What should you do before buying?

choices.text: Test it on your own real tasks
Ask the vendor if it works

questions.correct_answer: Test it on your own real tasks
questions.intro: Marketing makes every tool sound essential. Ask what problem it solves that your current tools do not. Try free trials with a reminder to cancel, and test on your real tasks, not the vendor's demos. Review subscriptions every few months and cancel unused ones. If a tool becomes central to your work, check how you would export your data if you ever leave, so you are not locked in.

questions.prompt: What helps with free trials?
